extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on working with traditional and new media, selecting channels (newspapers, wire services, magazines, syndicates) and best practices for distributing news and managing relationships with journalists and gatekeepers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled vs. uncontrolled (earned) media
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlled media include those in which practitioners have the say over what is said, how it is said, when it is said, and—to some extent—to whom it is said. Uncontrolled media—sometimes called “earned media”—are those over which practitioners have no direct role in decisions about media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the distinction and use controlled media when you need message control; rely on earned media for credibility and reach but accept gatekeepers decide content, emphasis, timing, and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust strategy for audience fragmentation and interactivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Three key changes: (1) audiences have become fragmented, choosing ever smaller niche media; (2) audiences are more active, choosing two-way media that permit interactivity; (3) a 'citizen journalist' today is anybody with a camera cell phone and Internet access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan campaigns that target niche outlets and interactive channels; factor in the role of nonprofessionals (citizen journalists) and two-way engagement when selecting channels and crafting messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know media gatekeepers' values and production requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must understand the role of information, the various media and their production requirements, and the values of the gatekeepers who control access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor content to mechanical constraints (space/time/formats), editorial values, and the business incentives (e.g., delivering audiences to advertisers). Failure to respect these leads to low placement or miscoverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match media type to message and target publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional mass media and magazines provide channels to reach large or narrowly defined audiences; newspapers reach literate, opinion-leading audiences while magazines allow targeting of shared interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select newspapers for broad influence and credibility, magazines for narrowly targeted interest groups, and wire/syndicate distribution for wide and timely reach. Use local papers for community publics and national outlets for high-level influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide complete context and background to reporters (especially inexperienced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because newsroom staffs may be young and overworked, the PR person must provide fundamental background and context rather than assume the reporter has institutional memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deluge the reporter with information, stress availability to answer questions, and insist the client be treated fairly (including opportunity to comment on allegations). Provide needed context proactively to avoid one-sided or inaccurate stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be accessible and responsive to journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters are easier to reach (emails, cell numbers) and are under pressure to publish in real time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear contact information, answer promptly, and be prepared for immediate follow-ups; timely accessibility can shape the accuracy and tone of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wire services for time-critical, wide distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial public relations wires (e.g., PR Newswire, Business Wire) electronically transmit text, photographs, audio and video news releases and regulatory postings to media and organizations for a fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paid distribution when you need simultaneous, fast transmission (e.g., recalls, earnings reports); wires can increase acceptability and reach but involve fees and options that affect distribution scope. They also sell monitoring/measurement services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage wire and syndicate credibility and reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Being carried by a wire service or syndicate increases the acceptability of the practitioner’s copy and ensures wide, economical distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For stories with broader geographic relevance or for features/photos, consider placing via wire services or syndicates to reach many outlets; understand differences among AP, Reuters, UPI, and commercial syndicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize newspapers' continued agenda-setting power and credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers remain powerful in shaping the public agenda and influencing debate; editorial pages remain a forum for political discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue newspaper coverage (news stories, opinion pieces, op-eds) for issues requiring depth, explanation, or to influence opinion leaders; use editorial placement strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and compensate for newsroom time pressures and errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The rush to publish on the web leads to less research, shallower thinking, poorer editing and more mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide accurate, verified information and background; monitor coverage and correct errors quickly; insist on fairness and opportunity to respond when allegations are published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand newspapers' mechanical constraints and content mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers have limited columns and fixed capacity; typically about 50 percent of space to editorial matter, with the rest as advertising and unpaid public service. Local news makes up the largest proportion (about 75%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limited space/time when pitching; craft succinct, newsworthy angles suitable for the outlet and consider local vs. national placement based on content relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Sunday supplements and weeklies for feature-oriented material
rubrics_metrics.description: Sunday papers emphasize feature material (stories without a time element) and weeklies emphasize local government, nonprofit, schools, sports, and personal news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch deeper, evergreen features to Sunday supplements; use weeklies for community-focused stories, human interest items, and announcements like births/weddings/obituaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience demographics when selecting media
rubrics_metrics.description: Readership varies by age, education, income, and race (e.g., higher newspaper readership among older adults, college graduates, and higher-income heads of household).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target media placements that match the demographic profile of your intended publics (e.g., use newspapers to reach older, higher-income, more-literate audiences; select niche magazines for specific interest groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor economic and ownership factors affecting media behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Economics, ownership consolidation, and alliances (newspapers sharing ownership with broadcast/cable) change newsroom resources and content-sharing practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate how shared ownership and resource constraints may influence coverage and tailor outreach (provide fuller context, multimedia assets) to increase chance of pickup across platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance new media with traditional media in the media mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite claims that 'traditional media are dead,' audiences still consume television and newspapers; traditional media remain core to public relations practice for many purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both traditional outlets (for depth, credibility, reach) and new/social media (for interactivity, niche targeting, speed) in campaign plans; do not abandon newspapers simply because of new channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize free/sponsored feature services as distribution options
rubrics_metrics.description: Some feature services supply material without charge (sponsored by clients) to many publications (e.g., NAPS), distributing consumer news, video news releases, B-roll, and scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider sponsored feature services when budget-constrained or when targeting many smaller outlets, but be aware sponsorship may affect perceived editorial independence and acceptability.
